problems.source_says: The paper describes three of the five judges only as authors not involved in app development and says nothing about the other two. It never calls the judges experts or gives them domain expertise (the topic is food waste; the authors are informatics researchers). The codebook defines expert_raters as domain experts, instructors, or professionals and human_raters as lay raters or crowd workers, and other forms code student research assistants as human_raters (c035 S1-O5, c150 S1-O1). The text supports the code for at most three of five judges. The form's open_questions flags this, but the measure field records expert_raters without qualification.
problems.quote: Shortlisted ideas were evaluated independently by five blind-to-condition judges, including the three authors not involved in app development, on a 7-point Likert scale.

problems.source_says: The text prints p = 0.015, but the cited Fig. 7a marks the human-fluency difference '**', and the Fig. 7 caption defines ** as p < .01. The paper contradicts itself. The form records the text value, which is correct as printed, but cites Fig. 7a as support without noting the conflict, which the later audit will meet. Every Fig. 8 marker agrees with its text p-value.

problems.locator: Text: PDF p. 12 (journal p. 1034), Sect. 4.1; figure: Fig. 7a and caption, PDF p. 13 (journal p. 1035)

confirmed: Assignment and AI availability: people were randomly assigned; in human + GLM the GLM could be used throughout the 10-minute session, and the shortlist of four was chosen right after from the same long list, so ai_available_when_produced = yes and timing = immediate hold for S1-O1 to S1-O8 (PDF p. 9, Sect. 3.2 and Fig. 4; PDF p. 8, Sect. 3.1).

Criterion 3: fluency is counted from session interaction data, flexibility is coded by a blind-to-condition student assistant, and novelty and value are rated by five blind judges on 7-point scales and averaged per participant (ICC(C,k) 0.864 and 0.736). None is self-reported (PDF p. 11, Sects. 3.5-3.6).

Levels: the human level keeps only ideas that originate from the human; the dyad level adds copied GLM ideas; GLM ideas not copied are not counted; for human-only, dyad performance equals individual performance (PDF p. 6, Figs. 2-3; PDF p. 11, Sect. 3.5).

Question: no task follows AI removal, and no measure compares different people's outputs; flexibility counts categories within one session; homogenization appears only as future work. So with_ai is correct for S1-O1 to S1-O8, and no across_people or after_ai outcome is missing (PDF p. 11, Sect. 3.5; PDF p. 17, Sect. 5.1.1).

Constructs: novelty is 'how novel, original or surprising the idea is'; value is 'how useful the idea is' (usefulness); fluency is the number of ideas; flexibility is the number of categories in one session, which the codebook calls flexibility, not diversity (PDF p. 11, Sect. 3.5).

Unit participant for S1-O1 to S1-O8: novelty and value are averaged per participant, flexibility is computed per session, dyad novelty has t(73), and the printed rB values equal 2U/(38 x 37) - 1 for S1-O1 (-0.324), S1-O5 (0.371), S1-O6 (0.536), and S1-O8 (0.414) (PDF pp. 11-13, Sects. 3.5, 4.1-4.2).

S1-O9 and S1-O10: the printed rB values equal 2U/(224 x 59) - 1 (0.461 and 0.600), so each test compares 224 human-origin with 59 GLM-origin shortlisted ideas (unit output, n_units 283). One arm has at most 4 x 38 = 152 shortlist slots, so the human-origin ideas span both arms; ai_available_when_produced = mixed and question = none (form-spec field note) hold (PDF p. 12, Sect. 4; PDF p. 14, Sect. 4.4).

Reported numbers: every U, t, p, d, rB, mean, and median recorded for S1-O1 to S1-O10, including the GPT-4 and Good-Idea-Count variants, matches the PDF text; dyad-novelty d = 0.667 agrees with t(73) = 2.889 and groups of 38 and 37 (PDF pp. 12-14, Sects. 4.1, 4.2, 4.4).

Directions: Table 2 gives the condition with higher performance as human-only for 1-a, none for 1-b to 1-d, and human + GLM for 2-a to 2-d, which matches treatment_lower, no_clear_difference, and treatment_higher in the form (PDF p. 15, Table 2).
Exclusions: four human + GLM participants who shortlisted none of their own ideas were dropped from human-level novelty and value; the paper does not print 71 (PDF p. 12, Sect. 4.1).

No missing outcomes: NASA-TLX cognitive load, cognitive stimulation, and felt responsibility are self-reports; the correlations are within one arm; GPT-4 ratings and the Good-Idea-Count are presented as robustness checks and are correctly folded in under form rule 7 (PDF pp. 11, 13-16, Sects. 3.5, 4.1-4.4).
Fig. 8 significance markers (** for p = 0.006, 0.005, 0.002; *** for p < 0.001) agree with the text, and the Fig. 8c interval plot does not state its interval type (PDF p. 13, Fig. 8 and Sect. 4.2).
summary: The outcome coding is supported on question, construct, unit, AI availability, direction, and every printed number: all ten outcomes are scored on the ideas participants produced (counted fluency, assistant-coded flexibility, judge-rated novelty and value), and rank-biserial arithmetic confirms participant-level tests for S1-O1 to S1-O8 and idea-level tests of 224 vs 59 ideas for S1-O9 and S1-O10. I mark it refuted only on two details that leave eligibility intact: the expert_raters code lacks support for the two undescribed judges, and the form cites Fig. 7a for human fluency without noting that the figure marks p < .01 while the text prints p = 0.015.
